rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A lamp that looks steady to a human can look like it is flashing to a European pied flycatcher, which sees flicker at up to about 145 flashes a second, where a human stops seeing it at about 60. A blue tit has been measured at about 130 flashes a second and an Anna's hummingbird at 70 to 80. For most other birds, nobody has measured how fast you see, so if you are not one of these three, your number is not known.
rows.note: Left out the compiled values (starling, cowbird, sparrow, owls) to keep the row short; they could be added as "a review reports".

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: For most birds, nobody has measured how sharply you see. If you are a house sparrow, you read about 5 cycles a degree, and if you are a mallard, about 12 (an estimate from the density of cells in the retina), where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart. If you are a Eurasian magpie or a western jackdaw, a compilation of behavior tests gives about 30, close to a human.
rows.note: No record for spacing of light-sensing cells (interreceptor_deg), so it is left out; figures stay with the species named.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In the blue tit, the European starling and the Eurasian blackbird, one kind of color-sensing cell peaks in it, between 360 and 375 nanometers, and a review table gives 315 nanometers as the point where the blue tit's lens and cornea pass half the light, so if you are a songbird you very likely sense ultraviolet. If you are a mallard, the matching cell peaks at 415 nanometers, in violet, and if you are a cormorant you very likely get almost no ultraviolet, since the lens and cornea of the pied cormorant block it.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "a review table gives". Left out the house sparrow (R13 is not its ultraviolet cell), the goldfinch's 399 nm and the great cormorant's 405 nm cell to keep the row short.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a red-winged blackbird, your two eyes together take in about 315 degrees, nearly a full circle, and they overlap over about 50 degrees in front of you. If you are a mallard, the overlap in front is about 20 degrees. For most other birds, including house sparrows and American robins, nobody has measured how wide you see.
rows.note: Kept to species with measured records; other measured species (mallard total, goldfinch, grebe, anhinga) left out for length.
